description: Regulatory and permitting risk factors affecting data center development. Critical in 2024-2026 as multiple jurisdictions have implemented moratoriums or heightened scrutiny. Data reflects publicly reported policy actions through early 2026.

metrics_explained.active_moratorium: Whether the jurisdiction has an active DC moratorium or building pause.
metrics_explained.moratorium_risk: Likelihood of future moratorium based on community opposition patterns. 1=low, 5=imminent.
metrics_explained.noise_ordinance_strict: Whether local noise regulations pose constraints on generators/cooling equipment.
metrics_explained.nimby_precedent: History of rejected or delayed DC applications in the jurisdiction.

Northern Virginia.notes: Prince William County rejected PW Digital Gateway expansions in 2024. Loudoun increased setback requirements. Growing community pushback, though no formal moratorium yet.

Dallas-Fort Worth.notes: Texas is broadly supportive. Some suburban pushback but state-level policy remains favorable.

Silicon Valley.notes: CEQA environmental review adds significant time. Santa Clara has capacity planning restrictions.

Phoenix.notes: Chandler tightening water use approvals. West Valley remains supportive.

Chicago.notes: Elk Grove Village has well-defined DC overlay. Suburban markets straightforward.

Atlanta.notes: Douglas County and state government supportive. Limited community opposition to date.

New York/New Jersey.notes: Dense urban environment creates friction. NYC has complex land use process.

Columbus.notes: New Albany has DC-supportive zoning. State and county actively courting investment.

Hillsboro-Portland.notes: Oregon UGB and land use planning adds complexity. Prineville remote but supportive.

Reno-Sparks.notes: TRIC (Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center) has entitlements in place. Nevada state welcoming.

Salt Lake City.notes: Eagle Mountain has DC-ready zoning. Utah generally supportive.

Minneapolis-St. Paul.notes: Generally smooth; suburban markets have DC overlays.

Austin-San Antonio.notes: Austin environmental considerations. San Antonio more straightforward.

Kansas City.notes: Historically welcoming. KC Industrial District has DC overlay.

Nashville.notes: Growing acceptance. Rutherford and Williamson counties favorable.

Denver.notes: Denver metro environmental scrutiny growing. Aurora more straightforward.

Richmond.notes: Follows NoVA precedent but less intense community opposition to date.

default_for_non_market.notes: Non-DC market. Limited precedent; outcomes depend on local political context.

national_trends: Community opposition to data centers has grown significantly through 2024-2025. Grid strain, water use, and neighborhood compatibility are primary concerns. Several jurisdictions have imposed pauses on new DC approvals pending utility and planning studies.
